articles.title: Belgian quarry uses 3,240 solar panels and sheep in a 3.3-hectare agrivoltaic project and produce clean power while preserving farmland
articles.summary: A quarry in Florennes, Wallonia, is combining solar power with sheep farming in a 3.3-hectare agrivoltaic project.
articles.body: A quarry in Florennes, Wallonia, is combining solar power with sheep farming in a 3.3-hectare agrivoltaic project. Calcaires Agri Énergie, in partnership with Ether Energy, developed the project, which places 3,240 photovoltaic panels above land used for sheep grazing. The panels have a total capacity of 2.27 MWc and are raised above the ground with six-metre gaps between them. According to the etherr.a, this layout allows sheep to graze beneath the installation while receiving protection from the weather. The project is designed to produce 2.33 GWh of electricity each year. The electricity will power the Calcaires de Florennes quarry, with the surplus supplied to the public grid. The project also includes plans to create a renewable energy community.How the Belgian quarry project supports both solar power and sheep farmingThe agrivoltaic project is located north of the Calcaires de Florennes quarry in Wallonia. It was developed by Calcaires Agri Énergie in partnership with Ether Energy. The installation covers 3.3 hectares and combines renewable electricity production with sheep farming. A total of 3,240 photovoltaic panels have been installed, with a capacity of 2.27 MWc. The panels cover 45% of the land. They are raised above the ground and positioned six metres apart.This arrangement leaves space for sheep to graze beneath the panels. The project also aims to preserve the agricultural role of the land while producing renewable energy. It supports farming through a partnership with the Grand-Bois farm in Gerpinnes. This setup combines electricity production with sheep farming.The project supports sheep farming in WalloniaThe solar panels are arranged to keep the land suitable for sheep grazing. They are installed at a height that allows the animals to move beneath them, while six-metre spacing between the panels leaves space for grazing. The project description says this setup allows the animals to graze freely below the solar installation.This setup allows the land to support both sheep grazing and solar power generation. The project supports extensive sheep farming and aims to help relocate sheep farming in Wallonia. The partnership with the Grand-Bois farm in Gerpinnes is part of that approach. The project notes that this provides a local alternative to imports, which account for more than 80% of the mutton consumed in Belgium.Reduce the quarry’s carbon footprintThe installation is expected to produce 2.33 GWh of electricity each year. The electricity will be used to power the activities of the Calcaires de Florennes quarry, helping reduce its dependence on the grid. The site will directly use some of the electricity produced by the panels.The remaining electricity is intended for the public grid and can cover the needs of approximately 225 households. The solar installation is also expected to help reduce the quarry’s overall carbon footprint by avoiding 2,000 tonnes of CO₂ emissions each year.Supporting farming and biodiversityThe project goes beyond electricity generation by including measures linked to agriculture and biodiversity. It is designed to support extensive sheep farming while keeping the land in agricultural use. The project notes that the approach helps preserve local biodiversity through extensive farming practices and natural features.It also plans to create a Renewable Energy Community. The project has been designed for a period of 30 years and is described as fully reversible. articles.title: Air India pilot found tipsy just before operating Zurich-Delhi flight, suspended
articles.summary: NEW DELHI: Air India has suspended a pilot who was reportedly found tipsy when he was to operate a Zurich-Delhi flight earlier this month.
articles.body: NEW DELHI: Air India has suspended a pilot who was reportedly found tipsy when he was to operate a Zurich-Delhi flight earlier this month. The Zurich-Delhi flight of Sept 6 had to be rescheduled after the pilot was found unfit to operate the same and till alternate crew was arranged. With the airline having faced similar issues in the past few months, the Directorate General of Civil Aviation (DGCA) has asked it to improve its checks and balances. The India regulator was apprised of the Zurich case by its Swiss counterpart."In the recent Zurich case involving a cockpit crew member, the individual was immediately removed from operating duties upon receipt of a preliminary breath analyser test report from local authorities and referred for further medical evaluation. The employee was subsequently repatriated to India as a passenger and remains under suspension pending the final medical examination report and completion of the investigation. Appropriate disciplinary action will be taken based on the findings," said an AI official.The airline, which recently terminated a pilot who had failed dope test after operating a badly rattled aircraft to Delhi, has seen multiple cases of tipsy pilots in the recent past. This Jan a pilot was detained at Vancouver airport after reeking of alcohol just before operating a flight to India.AI, whose safety practices are under the lens since last June Ahmedabad crash, says it "maintains an uncompromising commitment to safety, regulatory compliance and professional conduct across all aspects of its operations.""The airline follows a zero-tolerance policy towards any violation of safety, security or regulatory requirements. Any confirmed breach of established protocols is dealt with firmly, with disciplinary action taken in accordance with applicable regulations and company policies. This approach is consistent with Air India's longstanding policy that safety-related violations, particularly those involving alcohol, prohibited substances or conduct that could compromise operational safety, are treated with the utmost seriousness," the official added.Following the recent instances of crew failing dope and breath analyser (for alcohol) tests, AI says it has "has reinforced its expectations of professional conduct and regulatory compliance through multiple interventions across the organisation. A communication from the head of flight operations was issued to all pilots reiterating the airline's zero-tolerance policy towards the use of prohibited substances and reporting for duty under the influence of alcohol or drugs.""The communication underscored the responsibilities associated with operating an aircraft and reaffirmed that there can be no compromise on safety, integrity or regulatory compliance.... Air India conducts regular awareness and compliance programmes for pilots and other employees (focussing on) regulatory obligations and licensing requirements; professional conduct standards; substance abuse regulations....."Get the latest India News and Live updates. articles.title: From Ukraine to Africa, drone dog fights now a reality
articles.summary: The rapid proliferation of attack drones and loitering munitions on modern battlefields is pushing militaries around the world towards a new layer of air
articles.body: The rapid proliferation of attack drones and loitering munitions on modern battlefields is pushing militaries around the world towards a new layer of air defence — using drones to hunt down other drones. The ongoing Russo-Ukrainian conflict, which is characterised by drone warfare, has been the biggest driver of this shift. Ukraine has increasingly relied on interceptor UAVs to bring down Russian Shahed-type one-way attack drones, a tactic aimed at conserving costlier surface-to-air missiles for higher-value targets. Sudan's army, using a Turkish origin Akinci drone, has even shot down a Chinese-made CH-95 drone operated by UAE-backed Rapid Support Force.Interceptor drones work by detecting, chasing and neutralising hostile UAVs, either through direct collision, small onboard warheads or guided engagement systems. Unlike traditional air defence missiles, most of these interceptors are cheap to build and can be manufactured at scale, making them an attractive option against swarms of low-cost enemy drones.Ukraine has become the primary testing ground for this emerging technology. Ukrainian firms such as Wild Hornets have fielded systems like the Sting interceptor, built specifically to pursue and destroy incoming attack drones. Kyiv has also been linking interceptor UAVs to radar networks and command systems to sharpen detection, tracking and engagement.The next frontier is autonomous interception. In June 2026, Ukraine's Brave1 defence innovation programme confirmed the combat testing of an AI-assisted system, which fuses radar data with onboard recognition software to track Shahed-type drones while keeping a human in the loop.This area of warfare, like others is also experiencing an arms race where the development of a system leads to a counter-system and this cycle continues with each side one upping the other. In this scenario, newer jet-powered attack drones are cutting down reaction time, forcing Ukraine to develop faster interceptors and sharper guidance systems. Swarm tactics, jamming and the difficulty of spotting low-flying drones greatly add to the complications.Other major powers are pursuing similar systems. The United States has deployed its Merops counter-drone system along NATO's eastern flank and tested the Bumblebee interceptor, which uses automatic target recognition. Israel and several European nations are also building out aerial interception capabilities as part of broader counter-drone architectures.India, too, is building its own answer to the threat. The DRDO-BEL D4 system combines radar, electro-optical sensors and electronic warfare to detect and neutralise hostile UAVs, though this remains distinct from a dedicated interceptor drone built to physically engage airborne targets. Separately, DRDO completed development trials of its Unmanned Aerial Vehicle Launched Precision Guided Missile-V3 in May 2026, covering both air-to-air and air-to-ground modes, this step that could feed into future aerial interception and can be deployed as an anti-drone weapon.The learnings from Operation Sindoor have provided greater impetus to indigenous unmanned platforms and counter-UAS systems, as India works towards a layered defence combining radars, electronic warfare, interceptor drones, low-cost missiles and conventional weapons.

articles.title: A Texas oil geologist first saw McKittrick Canyon in 1921, later bought the land for a private retreat; 38 years later he donated 4,942 acres and his home, helping create Guadalupe Mountains National Park
articles.summary: In 1921, Texas oil geologist Wallace Pratt travelled into a remote, wind-swept oasis in West Texas and fell in love with its tall limestone walls and
articles.body: In 1921, Texas oil geologist Wallace Pratt travelled into a remote, wind-swept oasis in West Texas and fell in love with its tall limestone walls and bright autumn colours. Thirty-eight years later, his long love for McKittrick Canyon helped change the future of Texas conservation. Pratt gave his home and thousands of acres to the federal government, creating the core of what would become Guadalupe Mountains National Park.First encounter with a hidden oasisPratt was working as an oil geologist for Humble Oil Company when he first visited the region. He was on a business trip in 1921 when an associate, Judge Drane, introduced him to the Guadalupe Mountains. Pratt was soon given a chance to see McKittrick Canyon, which was described to him as “the most beautiful spot in Texas.” According to National Park Service history records, he was deeply impressed by both the scenery and the geology. The canyon cuts through part of the ancient Capitan Reef, a huge fossil reef formed about 265 million years ago. The reef developed when this part of Texas was covered by a tropical sea. For Pratt, who spent his career studying rocks and underground formations, the canyon was both a scientific treasure and a peaceful place to escape. Pratt soon decided to buy land there. He and two business partners purchased ranch property in the area. By 1930, Pratt had bought the remaining interests from his original partners and continued adding land, including the lower part and mouth of McKittrick Canyon. He called the property Manzanital Ranch.Building in the desert wildernessBy 1931, Pratt and his wife, Pearl Stuckey, had built a small stone cabin inside McKittrick Canyon. The cabin was designed by architect John Staubs and built during the winter of 1931 to 1932. Made from local stone, it became the Pratt family's summer home. The cabin was beautiful but its location had problems. The narrow canyon could be hit by strong floods and bad weather. Pratt began looking for a safer site on higher ground. After Pearl died in 1940, Pratt married Iris Calderhead in 1941. Calderhead was a prominent supporter of the women's suffrage movement and had been involved with the National Woman's Party. Soon after their marriage, the couple began planning a second home outside the canyon. They chose a site southeast of the canyon mouth. The New York City architecture firm Milliken & Bevin designed the house. Planning began in 1941, construction started in 1942, and the house was completed by 1943. The unusual home became known as “Ship on the Desert” because its long shape and modern design made it look like an oil tanker. It used local limestone and large areas of glass to connect the house with the surrounding landscape. The National Park Service describes it as an early example of modernist architecture in the remote West Texas region. The house also reflected the lives of both owners. Its ship-like design was a tribute to Pratt's career in the oil industry. An oil tanker, the Wallace E. Pratt, had been named after him in 1937. A bright purple front door was a nod to Iris Pratt's work for women's suffrage, since purple was one of the colours linked to the suffrage movement and the National Woman's Party.A landmark gift to the nationWallace and Iris Pratt lived at Ship on the Desert for about fifteen years. Their life there was quiet and remote. The house had no telephone or television during their years of occupation, but the family enjoyed the wide desert views and sunsets from the property. Although the Pratts were officially retired by 1945, Wallace continued to work from an office in Carlsbad, New Mexico. He often flew his small plane from a private runway near the house to his office. The family also operated Manzanital Ranch from the property, and Pratt's children and grandchildren often visited during the 1940s and 1950s. By the early 1960s, the Pratts moved to Tucson, Arizona, as Iris's health declined and the couple needed better access to medical care. Pratt had already begun thinking about the future of his land. He wanted McKittrick Canyon and the Guadalupe Mountains to remain protected. In 1959, Pratt began donating his property to the federal government. His first gift included 4,942 acres of land and Ship on the Desert. Between 1960 and 1961, the Pratt family donated another 690 acres. The total contribution reached more than 5,600 acres. National Park Service records describe Pratt's land as the starting point for the creation of Guadalupe Mountains National Park.The foundation of a national parkFederal officials saw the value of Pratt's gift and continued working to protect a much larger part of the Guadalupe Mountains. The government later acquired additional land, including a large holding owned by J. C. Hunter Jr., to build the larger park. Congress approved legislation for Guadalupe Mountains National Park in 1966. The land transfer was completed by 1970, and the park was formally dedicated and opened to the public in September 1972. Today, Guadalupe Mountains National Park protects 86,416 acres of desert, canyons, mountains, and other high-country landscapes. The park includes Guadalupe Peak, the highest point in Texas. Pratt's original property became an important part of that larger protected area. His decision to give up his private land helped make it possible for the public to experience the landscape he had come to value so deeply.Preservation and public accessThe buildings Pratt created remain important historic parts of the national park. Pratt Cabin, located at the meeting point of the North and South branches of McKittrick Canyon, is now an interpretive site and rest stop for hikers. The National Park Service uses the cabin to tell the story of the Pratt family and their years in the canyon. Ship on the Desert is also preserved by the National Park Service. The house is listed on the National Register of Historic Places and is recognised as an early example of modernism in West Texas. It is generally closed to the public because of preservation needs. The house still shows the personal touches that connected Pratt's life to the building. Its long form recalls the oil tanker named for him, while its purple front door reflects Iris Pratt's connection to the women's suffrage movement. McKittrick Canyon remains an important place for geologists because its exposed rock layers reveal the structure of the ancient Permian reef. It is also a popular destination for visitors, especially in autumn, when the canyon's trees add bright colour to the surrounding desert landscape.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. articles.title: Trump: Xi ‘seemed to like’ calling AI ‘super intelligence’
articles.summary: President Trump said on Friday that Chinese President Xi Jinping appeared to like referring to artificial intelligence as “super intelligence” days after Trump announced the U.S. would be using the new name in official documents and communications. Trump made the observation in a Truth Social post in which he referred to his meeting with the…
articles.body:
President Trump said on Friday that Chinese President Xi Jinping appeared to like referring to artificial intelligence as “super intelligence” days after Trump announced the U.S. would be using the new name in official documents and communications.

Trump made the observation in a Truth Social post in which he referred to his meeting with the Chinese leader as “very productive.”

“Tremendous things will be happening. Like almost everyone else, he seemed to like calling the poorly and inaccurately named Artificial Intelligence to a far more accurate and important name, SUPER INTELLIGENCE. That would be ‘SUPER!’ Everyone last night agreed, also,” Trump wrote.

Xi addressed the issue of artificial intelligence publicly at the White House on Thursday he but notably did not refer to it as superintelligence.

“We have both the capability and responsibility to develop and manage AI for good, and ensure that the development of AI is always under human control and serves the well-being of the people,” Xi said.

Superintelligence is already defined as a form of artificial intelligence that exceeds human intelligence. It is both the ultimate goal of many frontier AI firms and the greatest worry among those warning about its threat to humanity.

Trump announced at the United Nations General Assembly earlier this week that the term would be used instead of artificial intelligence in U.S. documents.

The State Department has since directed its diplomats to use it in their communications going forward.

articles.title: Susan Sarandon, Hannah Einbinder among celebrities arrested outside UN headquarters
articles.summary: Multiple celebrities were detained outside the United Nations headquarters.
articles.body:
[Nexstar] — Multiple celebrities were detained outside the United Nations headquarters in New York on Thursday.

According to the The Associated Press , around 100 people were arrested near the building ahead of Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s speech to the U.N. General Assembly .

Specifically, Oscar-winning actress Susan Sarandon and “Hacks” star Hannah Einbinder were among the protestors detained, according to the advocacy group Jewish Voice for Peace.

This comes after both actresses had made their thoughts about Palestine and the Israel-Hamas war in Gaza public, Variety reports.

Sarandon appeared at the Venice Film Festival in September and commented on being shut out of Hollywood following her remarks about Palestine. The actress said, “I’ve still had movies taken away recently because there are agencies that are telling people not to hire me still.”

Einbinder also commented on Palestine at an appearance at the Cannes Film Festival.

“There is a greater toll in not speaking, and you just gotta have your priorities straight,” she said at the time. “I am under no impression that my one small career could ever measure up in comparison to even one human life.”

“So, you know, it’s an obligation, and I will always do it,” the actress added.

Sheeran had avoided politics during his career but became caught in the middle after Macklemore’s statements.

An emotional Sheeran apologized to fans at one show and admitted that the debate has cost him close, personal relationships.

articles.title: Pope Leo champions free press, dodges White Sox miracle question
articles.summary: Pope Leo XIV said Friday he welcomes journalists to chronicle his travels, in sharp contrast to President Donald Trump, who recently kicked three news outlets out of the White House before having to undo that ban.
articles.body: ABOARD THE PAPAL PLANE — Pope Leo XIV said Friday he welcomes journalists to chronicle his travels, in sharp contrast to President Donald Trump, who recently kicked three news outlets out of the White House before having to undo that ban. The leader of the world’s Catholics was asked about the White House’s most recent bout with America’s free press — and while the pontiff didn’t mention Trump by name, he said good and thorough news coverage “is very important.” A federal court on Thursday forced the Trump administration to temporarily restore CNN’s, MS NOW’s and Politico’s access to their White House workspaces. “I am very happy that here you are all welcome, and we have it all the way around for everybody,” the pope said. “Good coverage, I think, is very important, and we have it all the way around for everybody. Thank you.” On a lighter note, the Chicago-raised Leo smiled broadly when he was asked about his beloved White Sox qualifying for the MLB playoffs — an overachievement of near-biblical proportions considering that the South Siders lost 121 games as recently as 2024. “Some call it a miracle. Do you have anything to do with that?” a reporter asked. “No comment,” a smiling Leo said. “Great things happen in Chicago.” The White Sox won the 2005 World Series, and Fox television cameras caught a passing glimpse of fan Robert Prevost — the man who’d later become Cardinal Robert Francis Prevost and then the first American pope. Claudio Lavanga reported from aboard the papal plane, and David K. Li reported from New York City.

articles.title: 9 Years Late, The Tesla Semi Officially Hits The Road
articles.summary: Nearly nine years after Elon Musk first unveiled the all-electric Class 8 big rig, Tesla has officially begun initial customer deliveries of its long-haul Se...
articles.body:
Nearly nine years after Elon Musk first unveiled the all-electric Class 8 big rig, Tesla has officially begun initial customer deliveries of its long-haul Semi.

During a webcast event held at the automaker's manufacturing facility in Sparks, Nevada, company executives showcased production-spec trucks carrying the logos of launch partners including PepsiCo, DHL, and US Foods.

While Tesla did not disclose vehicle pricing or current assembly figures during the presentation, executives reiterated long-term targets to scale output to 50,000 Semis per year-equivalent to roughly 1,000 units a week. The expansion is projected to add over 3,000 jobs to the Nevada facility. Some of those figures might be ambitious if the Cybertruck saga is anything to go on.

Musk, who did not attend the live presentation in person, appeared via a pre-recorded video message to urge logistics operators to reserve units, noting that the order backlog remains substantial.

500-Mile Real-World Range and Battery Options

The electric commercial truck will be offered in two primary configurations:

Long-Range Variant: Rated for up to 500 miles of driving range on a single charge when fully loaded at an 82,000-pound Gross Combination Weight. Dan Priestley, Tesla's director of Semi truck engineering, noted on stage that the 500-mile figure represents real-world highway driving validated by fleet partners.

Standard-Range Variant: Delivers an estimated 325 miles of range per charge.

First revealed in 2017 with an initial target production date of 2019, the Semi faced multiple delays before entering limited pilot operations with PepsiCo in late 2022; since then, other Semis have been spotted with DHL, Costco, and Walmart branding. The first high-volume production trucks rolled off the line in April.

According to Reuters , logistics coalition ZET SCALE recently placed an order for 2,500 Tesla Semis, marking one of the largest single commitments for electric Class 8 trucks in North America. That order follows an agreement by Swedish freight technology firm Einride AB to integrate 500 Tesla Semis into its shipping operations.

Tesla is well positioned to leverage the Semi in the commercial freight sector as transport operators look to hedge against fluctuating diesel prices and satisfy corporate zero-emissions mandates.

articles.title: Discovery of 97 million files related to SAS inquiry 'regrettable', MoD says
articles.summary: It comes after the inquiry's chair called the disclosure - three years into the investigation - "troubling".
articles.body:
The discovery of 97 million documents more than three years into an inquiry investigating allegations that UK special forces committed war crimes in Afghanistan was a "regrettable failure", the Ministry of Defence has said.

The admission comes after the inquiry's chair, Lord Justice Haddon-Cave, called the discovery "troubling" and "extraordinary news".

The independent inquiry was established in 2022 to investigate alleged executions by members of the Special Air Service between 2010 and 2013, during so-called night raids targeting the Taliban. It has yet to produce any findings.

MoD lawyers were called to a hearing on Friday to explain why the documents from the period in question were not found sooner.

Haddon-Cave said he had taken the "exceptional step" of calling the hearing because of the disclosure and the "somewhat casual way" the MoD had informed his team.

Steven Gray KC, representing the MoD, said the ministry "apologises that it fell short".

The "failure was one of communication, not application", he said, adding that the ministry was working hard to search through documents across multiple IT systems and classifications at "huge expense".

Gray added that the department was taking steps to avoid any similar revelations happening in the future.

Lawyers acting for the bereaved families said it was "staggering" the documents came to light at such a late stage in the inquiry's work.

Within the new files, the MoD says it has identified thousands of potentially relevant documents, including images that appear to have been taken during a number of special forces operations under investigation by the inquiry.

However, it stressed that much of the material found would be unrelated to the inquiry's terms of reference.

The Independent Inquiry relating to Afghanistan (IIA) told the BBC it was yet to receive any of the new material.

How a British special forces raid went fatally wrong

Afghan inquiry into alleged SAS war crimes has already cost £58m, MoD figures show

Ex-UK Special Forces break silence on 'war crimes' by colleagues

SAS war crime evidence suppressed, inquiry hears

SAS troops carried out night-time arrest raids across Afghanistan during the conflict there, called Deliberate Detention Operations (DDOs), which were meant to target Taliban commanders and bombmakers, and collect material that could provide further intelligence about insurgent networks.

Following a night raid, members of the SAS and their support staff took photos of anyone killed, and collected mobile phones and other devices for intelligence purposes.

Forensic experts are examining these images to see whether the SAS's account of what took place during the operations fits with the ballistic evidence visible in the photographs.

The inquiry follows years of reporting by BBC Panorama, which revealed evidence that the SAS deliberately killed people who posed no threat , including children and handcuffed detainees during raids.

It has already heard evidence from senior UK military personnel who have said they believed the SAS carried out extrajudicial killings of Afghan civilians.

It has also heard concerns about the secrecy under which the SAS operated and that previous investigations into the allegations were ended prematurely.

Edward Craven KC, acting on behalf of the bereaved families, echoed the chair's comments on the newly discovered documents, saying the disclosure represented yet another example of the MoD frustrating the justice process.

Craven said that what mattered most to the bereaved families was getting the truth about the deaths of their loved ones.

Haddon-Cave said it was crucial that "any material of real relevance is quickly identified and disclosed", adding that he intended to call another hearing next month to question the MoD on its progress.

The MoD said it was fully committed to supporting the inquiry and that it regretted that it was "not as prompt or consistent as it should have been" in disclosing the documents.

Set up by the then-Defence Secretary Ben Wallace following the publication of the evidence by the BBC in 2022, the IIA has come under criticism over delays and mounting costs.

It had stated that it would provide an interim or final report 12-18 months after it was established in 2022. After almost four years, it has yet to publish any findings.

The BBC revealed earlier this month that it has already cost the public purse £58m.

Around half of that cost is understood to have been money spent by the MoD and the wider government in responding to the inquiry, including lawyers representing former SAS officers and senior military figures.

Public inquiries are rarely quick or cheap. The inquiry into the fire at Grenfell Tower, which claimed 72 lives and was found to be entirely avoidable, took more than seven years to complete and cost more than £170m.

Haddon-Cave said he had set a deadline to hear all evidence by 30 April 2027 and that he was seeking assurances that the new discovery would not delay the work of the inquiry further.

articles.title: More Americans than ever now have a positive view of socialism, new poll says
articles.summary: A new Gallup Poll shows 43% of Americans view socialism positively, with independents surging from 37% to 45% as big business approval plummets.
articles.body: More Americans than ever view socialism positively, according to a Gallup poll released Wednesday, as 43% view it positively for the first time since 2010. Gallup asked respondents if they have a positive or negative image of socialism, capitalism, free enterprise, big business and small business in the poll conducted in August. Fifty-five percent of Americans view capitalism positively. The poll's findings show a significant drop in how Americans view big business, which is down 14 points from 2010, free enterprise down 9 points and capitalism down 6 points. Small business is the only category that hasn't lost any support. SOCIALISM SURGES AMONG DEMOCRATS AS PARTY LEADERS REJECT DSA AGENDA: ‘PACK OF FOOLS’ The increase in socialism’s positive rating through 2025 was largely due to the views of Democrats, rising from 50% in 2010 to 66% last year. However, this year's increase is due to political independents, according to Gallup, whose positive rating jumped from 37% in 2025 to 45%. This year's findings show 65% of Democrats view socialism positively, compared with 14% of Republicans. FOX NEWS POLL: SQUEEZED BY COSTS, FRUSTRATED VOTERS TURN TO THE DEMOCRATS Lucas Holtz, a senior political advisor at Third Way, told Fox News Digital in a statement, "The Gallup poll isn't evidence of Americans embracing socialism—it's evidence that Americans are rejecting the economic status quo. When we look a single layer beneath to ask whether voters support socialist policies, support completely collapses." "Working-class Americans are pissed about the costs of everyday life and the economy, but it's off base to think that a majority of Democrats and independents would back wholesale DSA socialism," Holtz continued. JOE MANCHIN SAYS HE WOULD NEVER SUPPORT A SOCIALIST CANDIDATE, WARNS AGAINST 'CRAZY' POSITIONS Holtz pointed to a Third Way poll that found Democrats and Democratic-leaning independents prefer "capitalism with guardrails" over socialism by 24 points. "Echelon Insights also ran a poll and found that socialism is 33 points underwater with independents. And they found that a whole lot of DSA-aligned policies would make voters less likely to back a candidate. Abolishing police and prisons: 73% less likely (77% among independents). Ending all immigration detention and deportations: 43% less likely (42% among independents). Government ownership of major transportation and energy infrastructure: 39% less likely (44% less likely among independents)," Holtz said. The Gallup poll found that views of the economic systems differed by age group. Adults aged 18 to 34 view socialism more positively than capitalism, 57% vs. 43%, and those aged 55 and older view capitalism more positively than socialism, 65% vs. 34%. VANCE WARNS THERE WILL BE A 'SOCIALIST PRESIDENT IN THIS COUNTRY' IF GOP DOESN'T FIX ECONOMY FOR YOUNG PEOPLE Adults ages 35 to 54, however, rate socialism and capitalism about the same. A professor of political science at Northeastern University, Costas Panagopoulos, told Fox News Digital, "For Independents, whose views are driven least by partisan attachments, perceptions about socialism are gaining in favorability in part because they feel betrayed, overlooked or neglected by modern American capitalism." SOCIALISM’S RISE INSIDE THE DEMOCRATIC PARTY NOW THREATENS THE AMERICAN DREAM Gallup's summary of its poll read, "Capitalism, free enterprise and especially big business are viewed less positively than they once were, while socialism has gained ground. Those changes have been most pronounced among Democrats and younger adults, but this year's uptick in socialism's appeal reflects a novel shift among independents." CLICK HERE FOR MORE COVERAGE OF MEDIA AND CULTURE The poll comes amid a rise in socialist political candidates across the country, some of whom have won primary elections. articles.title: Tory ex-ministers face serious questions over migrant centre chaos, inquiry hears
articles.summary: The Manston centre in Kent became overwhelmed in November 2022 at the height of the small boats crisis.
articles.body:
An overcrowded migrant reception centre, where a man died, raises "very serious questions" for ministers in the former Conservative government, including two home secretaries and former prime ministers, an inquiry has heard.

The Manston centre in Kent became overwhelmed in November 2022 at the height of the small boats crisis, with around 4,000 people held there.

Home Office officials knew conditions were unlawful and children were at risk of harm, but had no alternative plan for where to accommodate them, the inquiry heard on Friday.

Former Home Secretaries Dame Priti Patel and Suella Braverman shared in preliminary evidence that Number 10 was involved in decisions made at the time.

The Manston centre, a former military site near Dover, was converted into an emergency holding facility for cross-channel migrants in early 2022, as small boat crossings began to soar.

It was designed to hold up to around 1,000 people at any one time and for no longer than a legal limit of 24 hours.

But by November 2022, thousands of people were sleeping in marquees and it was apparent that there was disease, illness and no adequate care for children traumatised by crossing the English Channel.

During this critical period, the government was hoping that it could eventually send asylum seekers to Rwanda.

As the number of detainees grew, doctors identified diphtheria was present - and that 31-year-old Iraqi Hussein Haseeb Ahmed was suspected of suffering from the highly dangerous disease, the preparatory inquiry hearing heard on Friday.

He was not immediately taken to hospital, but died on 19 November at 05:30 after he was admitted to hospital as his condition deteriorated.

"He was handcuffed until around 2am," Claire Dobbin KC, the inquiry's lead lawyer, said.

"His handcuffing in hospital at a point when he must have been close to death, all require separate examination."

At one stage, some 81 families were sharing one toilet with babies, children, teenagers and adults sharing the same space despite clear safety concerns, she said.

Some detainees had visible wounds. One person, who was not given medical care, was using a plastic croissant wrapper as a dressing.

"The position of children is a matter of great concern," said Dobbin.

"Generally the circumstances in which children can be detained in England are very limited indeed."

Dobbin added that one senior official at the Home Office told colleagues that the conditions were the worst he had seen in 20 years.

He wrote in an email: "Political decisions have forced hard-working officials and suppliers into an impossible position. This will end up as a public inquiry and rightly."

Other witnesses have said there was racism, hostility and aggression towards the detainees from some staff, with some accused of threatening to withhold meals from people who wanted to use the toilet.

"The body of evidence raises very serious questions for senior officials and ministers as to how the detention of children in these conditions was tolerated on humanitarian or legal grounds," said Dobbin.

Two former home secretaries involved in the Manston decision-making - Dame Priti and Braverman - have already provided evidence that will be examined in depth in future hearings.

Braverman's personal legal representative - who is paid for by the government - gave no statement on her behalf during Friday's session.

But the inquiry heard she had already explained in written submissions that Number 10 had been aware of the situation at Manston and that the decision to pause using hotels had led to the overcrowding.

It was also told there had been "prolonged periods of disengagement" from Robert Jenrick, the immigration minister in late 2022, although he had provided a statement.

It is not clear yet whether former Prime Ministers Boris Johnson or Rishi Sunak will be asked to give evidence about their roles.

The inquiry team will now continue gathering evidence with the date for full hearings yet to be fixed.

articles.title: From hiding in bomb shelters to visiting New York, Iran’s leaders seize the opportunity
articles.summary: Seven months after escaping with his life from a US-coordinated Israeli airstrike that killed Supreme Leader Ayatollah Ali Khamenei, Iran’s top diplomat walked the streets of Manhattan this week under the protection of the US Secret Service.
articles.body: Seven months after escaping with his life from a US-coordinated Israeli airstrike that killed Supreme Leader Ayatollah Ali Khamenei, Iran’s top diplomat walked the streets of Manhattan this week under the protection of the US Secret Service. As leaders gathered in New York for the UN General Assembly, Abbas Araghchi and Iran’s president, Masoud Pezeshkian, have seized the opportunity to make their case to the world, casting the Islamic Republic as a country abiding by international law against “bullies” who are not. Araghchi met with more than two dozen diplomats, including counterparts from more than ten European countries and even Jordan’s foreign minister, whose country Iran had attacked. More importantly, he held a rare direct meeting with US envoy Steve Witkoff and told western media that Iran had put a new offer on the table. In his address to the UN gathering, Pezeshkian said the Islamic Republic would never “bow down” – a line that landed well with hardliners at home, some of whom had opposed the trip at a time when war-time sanctions and a US naval blockade are choking Iran’s economy. On Thursday, Pezeshkian sat with Western journalists and think-tank analysts at a New York hotel to lay out his government’s thinking – a far cry from the morning of February 28, when he was feared dead after vanishing for hours amid waves of US-Israeli strikes. In previous decades, Iran’s turns at the United Nations General Assembly have garnered attention, but under the shadow of war, this year’s visit became the main event. Tehran’s officials planned the visit strategically , mindful of both global and domestic attention. Hardliners in Iran initially criticized Pezeshkian and Araghchi’s diplomatic overtures to Washington, deeming a decision to visit the country actively waging war against them as a sign of surrender. Araghchi, in particular, came under fire from Iran’s conservative lawmakers for meeting Witkoff. “Foreign policy and national security are not arenas for recklessness,” a hardline lawmaker, Ebrahim Rezaei, wrote on X Wednesday. “The foreign minister must explain on which authorization his meeting with the representative of the enemy was conducted?” Yet, despite the high risk of a political misstep, Iranian officials staged a visit that played well at home, revived a diplomatic track with their adversary, declared a message of survival to the world and delivered their thinking to the American public. Pezeshkian declared Iran’s demands from the UN podium and held bilateral meetings with his counterparts. By contrast, Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, who co-launched the war on Iran, was met with protests on the streets of New York and a mass walkout of UN delegates as he delivered his speech from the floor. Fresh proposal Araghchi’s meeting with Witkoff to restart talks was an attempt to break three months of diplomatic deadlock. Still, US officials were quick to caution that an agreement would take time. “If there’s going to be a deal with Iran…it’s going to involve a lot of hard work over a period of time, and it will engage and involve mediators as well,” Secretary of State Marco Rubio told reporters this week. Iran said it had presented a proposal to the US that would re-open the Strait of Hormuz - in return for Washington lifting its economic blockade of Iran - and restart the push towards a “final deal.” Tehran’s fresh offer requires Washington to meet a set of conditions within seven days, Araghchi told reporters. He declined to elaborate on those conditions but said that they were “nothing more” than what was included in the Memorandum of Understanding - an ill-fated agreement signed between both parties in June that quickly collapsed. While a swift reopening of the strait and a resumption of talks over Tehran’s nuclear program could be tempting to Trump, obstacles remain. Iran’s conditions include the US waiving sanctions on oil sales, lifting the naval blockade and ending other economic penalties imposed after the breakdown of the agreement back in June, a regional source familiar with the talks told CNN. In the new proposal, Iran wants Washington to take the first steps, an expert told CNN. “The offer now is essentially the same bargain, but with a very different sequence,” Sina Toossi, a senior fellow at the Center for International Policy in Washington, D.C told CNN. “The US takes concrete steps first, and only then does Iran ease its pressure over Hormuz.” Under the June deal, which at the time was widely seen as favorable to Iran, the US agreed to lift a naval blockade, end sanctions on the regime, set up a $300 billion fund to reconstruct the country and accept the Islamic Republic’s role in managing a narrow waterway where a fifth of global oil crosses daily. The agreement quickly collapsed after the Trump administration accused Tehran of firing on ships in the Hormuz. Iran, in turn, accused Washington of its own breaches by launching strikes on Iran and refusing to release cash frozen in banks abroad. “The central message from Pezeshkian’s New York trip is that Iran genuinely wants a deal,” Toossi added, “but it is no longer willing to strike a deal and de-escalate first and simply trust that Washington will follow through.” Iran has also pursued a separate diplomatic track with Oman, the only other country that borders the Strait of Hormuz, on how to manage the waterway. Iran has in the past demanded future payment for managing the Strait, but it remains unclear if that demand is part of Tehran’s new offer. It’s also unclear if the new Iranian-Omani framework has been presented to the Trump administration. An attempt to bring neighboring Arab states on board failed last week. One of the bigger lingering questions is whether Iran will accept a new negotiation that Washington could use to extract further concessions. Both sides are currently locked in a showdown over who can live with the status quo the longest. Iran is advertising a high pain threshold while Trump insists that he will not be hurt in the upcoming midterm elections even as gas prices climb at the pump. So, Tehran’s leaders might have had a good few days – but it is unclear how long the glow will last. “They’re waiting to see how I do in the midterm election,” Trump said in his speech at the UN. “What they don’t realize is that I’m not running. I did that already and won in a landslide.”

articles.title: Lake District space museum launched by Britain's first astronaut
articles.summary: Helen Sharman officially opened the John Dulcamara Space Flight Museum at Grizedale Observatory.
articles.body:
A new space flight museum has been opened at a Lake District observatory.

Britain's first astronaut Helen Sharman visited Grizedale Observatory and Planetarium on Friday to officially open the John Dulcamara Space Flight Museum.

The collection was donated by private collector John Dulcamara and includes a piece of the command module from the 1969 Apollo 11 - the first manned mission to land on the moon.

Sharman said the collection was "extraordinary".

Grizedale Observatory near Ambleside, Cumbria, opened in May 2024, offering public access to telescopes, a planetarium and meteorite laboratory, as well as staging a dark skies festival and other events.

Sharman, who became the first British person to visit space in 1991, said: "It's an extraordinary collection. We've got bits of Apollo 11, bits from the Russian space programme - it's just an amazing collection of artefacts from space flight history.

"It tells its own story of space history, but also of the people that went and the items that were important to them.

"For it to be on show now in this beautiful way, as part of Grizedale Observatory, what a coup for Cumbria."

The museum contains a variety of pieces ranging from autographed photos and signatures of prominent people in space flight to parts of actual space craft.

Dulcamara said he first started collecting the artefacts after he attended a shuttle launch in 1996 and kept the ticket.

"That's what started my 30 year collection off," he said. "There's thousands of pieces on display, I hope people will come and have a look."

Observatory director Gary Fildes said that the collection presented some "fascinating stories".

"John asked whether we would be interested in keeping his collection here at the observatory so other people could have the chance to see it. He brought a few samples along and we knew we had to make it happen.

"We thought: 'failure is not an option'!"

During her visit, Sharman met with local schoolchildren to talk about her time aboard the Mir Space Station, where she carried out scientific experiments and observations of Earth.

"To have Helen opening the museum is incredibly special," Fildes said. "What makes this particularly important to us is the opportunity for local children to meet Helen.

"You simply don't know where an experience like that might lead."

articles.title: Israeli shelling continues as Lebanon’s PM demands withdrawal in UN speech
articles.summary: Lebanese Prime Minister Nawaf Salam wants a US-brokered ceasefire to be consolidated and for Israel to retreat.
articles.body:
Lebanese Prime Minister Nawaf Salam has called for an end to the Israeli occupation of southern Lebanon and the full enforcement of the ceasefire, as Israeli shelling and demolitions continue.

“We want the war to end and we want the ceasefire [with Israel] consolidated,” Salam said in a speech at the United Nations General Assembly in New York on Friday.

The prime minister demanded a complete withdrawal of Israeli forces from Lebanese territory up to its internationally recognised border and the release of all Lebanese detainees.

As delegates gathered to listen to Salam, on the ground in Lebanon, Israeli forces carried out a large explosion near Taybeh and Deir Siryan, while an Israeli air strike targeted a valley between Froun and Ghandourieh, triggering a large fire.

Al Jazeera’s Zeina Khodr, reporting from Froun, said the reality on the ground is that the conflict is far from over.

“From the ground here in Froun, we can still see Israeli warplanes and drones flying at low altitudes in the skies above and Israeli artillery shelling is still causing uncontrollable fires. Lebanese civil defence and firefighters are not being allowed by the Israelis to reach these areas and put out the flames,” she said.

“More than 60 towns in southern Lebanon are still occupied by the Israeli army, where the Israelis are carrying out a systematic campaign of demolitions,” Khodr added.

Israeli forces are “blowing up people’s homes, despite the framework agreement in which there is supposed to be a ceasefire that they have signed with the Lebanese government,” she said.

Israeli attacks in southern Lebanon have killed at least 4,386 people and wounded 12,407 others since March 2 , when the current Hezbollah-Israel war started. Since then, Israeli forces have occupied up to 600sq km of Lebanese territory up to the Litani River.

A US-brokered framework agreement between Lebanon and Israel in June provides for a gradual Israeli withdrawal from Lebanese territory and the deployment of the Lebanese army in areas vacated by Israeli forces.

Speaking at the UNGA, Salam said his government had entered into negotiations with Israel, mediated by the United States and President Donald Trump, “to end the war and restore Lebanon’s sovereignty”, adding that the success of any agreement is measured not by intentions but by fulfilment of commitments.

“What is required is to complete the translation of this agreement into practical steps within a clear timetable and with a verification mechanism that ensures the implementation of all its provisions,” he said.

He focused on state sovereignty, saying it “cannot be untouchable in one place and negotiable in another, nor can the rules of international law apply to some but not to others”.

Salam also pledged to oversee the disarmament of Hezbollah in exchange for Israel’s eventual full withdrawal, also saying “weapons must be exclusively in the hands of the state and that decisions on war and peace rest solely with its constitutional institutions”.

Stability in the Middle East can only come with respect for Palestinian rights, he said.

“There can be no lasting stability in Lebanon without lasting stability in our region, and there can be no stability in the region as long as this organisation [the UN] remains unable to enable the Palestinian people to exercise their inalienable right to self-determination, like all other peoples of the world,” Salam said. “No less and no more.”

articles.title: Ole Miss toxicology reports expected soon and results may trigger anti-fentanyl law, official says
articles.summary: Toxicology reports in the Ole Miss deaths of Robert Strang and Aidan Hamilton could come within days as investigators weigh kratom and foul play.
articles.body: OXFORD, Miss. — Toxicology reports in the suspicious deaths of two University of Mississippi students are expected to be completed as early as next week, according to the state's commissioner of public safety, and Oxford police have separately announced arrests in connection with a raid on a tobacco shop accused of trafficking narcotics. The victims have been identified as Robert Strang, a 20-year-old junior from Atlanta, and Aidan Hamilton, an 18-year-old freshman from Colorado. Both families have asked for privacy and compassion as they mourn the loss of their sons. It remains unclear how the students died, but narcotics detectives are involved in investigations into both of their deaths. If the reports find fentanyl, there is a special Mississippi law that can be used to target whoever sold it, according to authorities. "Under Parker’s Law, enacted in 2022, criminal charges may be pursued when an unlawful delivery of fentanyl results in a person’s death," Sean Tindell, the commissioner of Mississippi's Department of Public Safety, told Fox News Digital. "If the investigation establishes those circumstances, law enforcement will work with prosecutors to pursue the appropriate charges and hold those responsible accountable." OLE MISS DEATHS, DRUGGINGS HAVE ‘PEOPLE SCARED TO LEAVE’ DORMS AS BARS, GREEK LIFE CLAMP DOWN: STUDENTS Separately, Oxford police have announced the arrests of two men in a narcotics investigation connected to a local tobacco shop. It's not immediately clear whether the raid has any connection to the student deaths. The suspects were linked to an Oxford retail business where police allegedly found stockpiles of drugs including THC products and kratom, which is legal in many parts of the country but not in Lafayette County. "During the search, agents recovered more than 500 units of kratom, along with an assortment of THC cartridges, gummies, and other suspected narcotics," police said in a statement. "Kratom has been prohibited from possession, distribution, and sale within the City of Oxford since 2019." SEND US A TIP The store is called Puffs Vape, Tobacco and Beer Store, located in the 100 block of Heritage Drive in Oxford. Oxford police arrested Yahya Mohamed Mosleh, 51, and Islam Mohamed, 18. Both are local residents. In 2022, the business owner, Amer Alowdi, 40, was indicted on narcotics trafficking charges and fled the country before being prosecuted, police said in a statement. It was not immediately clear how the business remained open. Tindell told Fox News Digital Thursday that while authorities haven't uncovered any indications of foul play, they haven't ruled it out either. "Until the autopsy is reported, and the investigators have an opportunity to get statements and collect evidence, then that final determination will not be made until later," he said. WHAT IS KRATOM? articles.title: Jersey chief minister says AI brings opportunities
articles.summary: Senator Lyndon Farnham says AI can boost productivity and help curb public sector growth.
articles.body:
Artificial intelligence (AI) could help to improve public services without putting existing jobs at risk and Jersey should seek to benefit from technological advances, the island's chief minister has said.

In his first major pitch to business leaders since his re-election as chief minister , Senator Lyndon Farnham said ministers would support local firms to adopt AI, and islanders to develop skills needed in modern workplaces.

Although AI had to be used "responsibly", he added, it could also support continuing efforts to curb growth in the public sector.

A recent series of warnings about the potential dangers of AI have led to calls for co-ordinated action to slow the technology's development .

"I think AI can bring a lot of opportunities," he said at a Chamber of Commerce lunch entitled A New Term, New Priorities.

"We're hearing from global news at the moment there are potential challenges and we have to be, I think, mindful of how we allow AI to develop and the control we give it.

"But there is certainly scope for it to bring greater productivity and improve services in the public sector and we're focusing on that and our digital team have started to roll that out already."

Farnham said he hoped increasing reliance on AI would not put existing public sector jobs at risk.

"What it will mean is we'll be able to do more with the resources we have," he said.

"In the past, we would just take on more resources to do more.

"I think becoming more productive, embracing the use of AI will allow us to do more work, but with the resources we have."

In addition to the role AI might play, Farnham said that a recruitment freeze introduced in August 2024 after the public sector workforce grew to its highest level since records began had already prevented "in the region of 500 new positions occurring, saving tens of millions of pounds".

He said his government had subsequently taken "1,000 job vacancies out of the system", and introduced restrictions on the use of consultancy and agency staff.

"So although the cost of government has increased, mainly in line, now, with inflation, we have certainly curbed the growth," he added.

Farnham told the audience of business leaders ministers could not ask businesses to become more efficient while allowing the public sector to grow.

"We will therefore maintain firm control over the size and the cost of government," he said.

"The recruitment restrictions introduced in the last term have helped control expenditure and refocus the workforce.

But Michael Van Neste, the former head of the Jersey Homes Trust, said the chief minister's speech could "easily" have been made decades earlier.

"When Frank Walker was the chief minister, he had an objective of reducing red tape and reducing the cost of the civil service," he told the BBC.

"Things have just got worse and worse and worse - and the cost of the civil service has to be sustainable.

"At the moment, there's a crude cap on recruitment to level-off the cost of the civil service."

He continued: "The very fact they've had to put a cap on recruitment is an indication that things are not really in control."

He said it was evident that Farnham wanted to curb public sector growth, but added: "I just wonder whether anyone in the current Council of Ministers has the leadership to achieve those objectives."

Speaking after she had listened to Farnham's speech, recruitment consultant Shelley Kendrick said that the "evolution of AI" had already led to changes in the ways private sector organisations worked.

"We see people on a weekly basis who are being made redundant," she said.

"There isn't jobs for them to go to, so what are we going to do about that?"

She said the government needed to do more to address skills shortages, which she claimed were affecting half of Jersey businesses.

In response, Farnham said there was a need for "even stronger links" between schools and Highlands College and employers, "so that we are developing the skills Jersey will need into the future".

He continued: "Artificial intelligence is already beginning to transform the way we work and do business.

"Jersey should not simply respond to that change - we should position ourselves to benefit from it.

"That means helping businesses adopt AI, developing the skills our workforce will need and using it responsibly within government to improve performance, efficiency and public services."

articles.title: Al Jazeera rejects Netanyahu’s attack on journalists in UN speech
articles.summary: Israeli PM’s criticism of Al Jazeera during UNGA address threatens safety of journalists, the media network says.
articles.body:
Al Jazeera has rejected Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s attack against the network during a speech at the United Nations General Assembly.

In a statement on Friday, Al Jazeera Media Network said it “categorically rejects” Netanyahu’s remarks, regarding them as the latest example of Israel’s “sustained campaign against Al Jazeera and its journalists”.

In his address at the UNGA on Thursday, where he attacked critics of Israel’s genocide in Gaza and pogroms in the occupied West Bank, Netanyahu singled out Al Jazeera. He called the network one of the world’s “toxic media outlets” that intends to “brainwash young minds to hate Israel”.

Al Jazeera said Netanyahu wanted to stop the outlet from “reporting facts from the ground, documenting events, providing context and ensuring that a range of voices and perspectives are heard”.

Further rejecting Netanyahu’s verbal assault, Al Jazeera said the fact that “such rhetoric was delivered from the podium of the United Nations is a matter of particular concern, given the threat such rhetoric poses to the safety of Al Jazeera journalists working in the field”.

“This rhetoric cannot be separated from the heavy toll borne by Al Jazeera’s journalists in Gaza,” the network’s statement added.

More than 270 journalists have been killed in Gaza during Israel’s genocidal onslaught. At least 12 of the victims had been reporting for Al Jazeera.

Al Jazeera said the network “has lost a number of journalists and camera operators while they were carrying out their work. Some were subjected to campaigns of incitement and vilification before being targeted”.

Of the more than 73,000 people killed in Gaza, at least 706 are family members of journalists of Palestinian journalists, according to the Palestinian Journalists Syndicate.

Israel has repeatedly cracked down on Al Jazeera and used pressure campaigns against Qatar.

Two years ago, Israel’s cabinet voted to shut down Al Jazeera in the country, immediately ordering the closure of its offices and a ban on the network’s broadcasts. This came after Israel’s Knesset passed a law allowing the government to temporarily close down foreign media outlets it deemed a “threat to security”.

“These measures do not target Al Jazeera alone; they also undermine the right of every person to access truthful information and independent journalistic coverage,” Al Jazeera said on Friday.

It added that “the role of journalism is to provide the world with facts and context, while respecting the right and ability of individuals to assess sources and form their own opinions.”

articles.title: Lebanese in Brazil, Brazilian in Lebanon
articles.summary: Their families left Lebanon generations ago. For some Lebanese Brazilians, Lebanon’s pull never disappeared.
articles.body:
Beirut, Lebanon – The techno beat falls away for a moment as the DJ lines up another song. Its opening chords pulse through the speakers and the room erupts. In the crush of the club, people cheer and scramble onto wooden tables and chairs, craning over one another for a better view of the woman stepping onto the dance floor.

As her white silk skirt floats around her, Naima Yazbek, 55, twirls to the sound of the classical Arabic song Alf Leila wa Leila (One Thousand and One Nights), letting the music carry her through every flick of the wrist, every spin.

At Madame Om, a bearded man with broad shoulders snaps a paper fan to the beat, his clapping setting off others around him. For the length of the song, no one appears particularly concerned about whether the woman before them can speak Arabic, which passport she carries, or where she was born. The crowd simply wants to watch her dance. Outside this room, those distinctions have followed Naima for years.

A few days before the performance, sitting beneath towering pine trees outside Cafe Younes in Beirut's Hamra neighbourhood, she crosses her tanned legs and lights a cigarette. Large black fans turn slowly around her, stirring the hot city air.

Between puffs of smoke, she explains that dance was bound up with another reason for coming to Lebanon: understanding the culture she had grown up knowing through her family.

“As a belly dancer and singer, I wanted to be here, [to] learn the language, the culture, [and] to understand my family roots.”

Born in Sao Paulo into a family of Lebanese descent, Naima says her relationship with Lebanon began long before she first set foot in the country in the summer of 2009. Like millions of Brazilians whose family histories stretch back to Lebanon, she inherited a relationship with a place she knew first through other people's memories. Eventually, she would decide to make that place home.

Naima's Christian ancestors were among those who left what was then Ottoman-ruled Greater Syria for Brazil in the late 19th century. Economic hardship, including the decline of Mount Lebanon's silk economy, helped drive migration to the Americas, where expanding economies offered the prospect of work and a different future.

The migration would eventually create one of the world's largest Lebanese diasporas. Brazil's foreign ministry estimates that as many as 10 million Lebanese people and their descendants now live in the country.

For generations, Naima's family built its life there, often marrying within the Lebanese diaspora. But the idea of Lebanon never entirely disappeared.

In 1928, her great-grandfather even persuaded his wife, Odete, to try living in Lebanon. The experiment lasted only a few months. He returned to Brazil, feeling that the Lebanon he encountered was no longer the country he remembered.

More than 80 years later, their great-granddaughter would make the same journey and reach a very different conclusion.

articles.title: US top court allows Trump to use controversial voter verification system
articles.summary: Voting rights groups have warned system may falsely identify voters as non-citizens, leading to disenfranchisement.
articles.body:
The United States Supreme Court has allowed the administration of US President Donald Trump to use a controversial voter verification system just weeks away from the midterm election in November.

The court’s emergency order on Friday allows the Department of Homeland Security to use the Systematic Alien Verification for Entitlements, or SAVE, programme in its efforts to verify the eligibility of voters on state voter rolls.

Voting rights groups have argued the use of the system, which was revamped under the Trump administration in 2025, risks falsely identifying individuals as non-voters, potentially leading to individuals being wrongfully purged from voter rolls.

Those challenging the administration’s use of the database have charged that information on citizenship can be out of date. They pointed to a Travis County, Texas election official who found that up to 25 percent of the “non-citizens” identified by the system in the jurisdiction were in fact US citizens.

US states oversee election administration under the country’s constitution and are not required to use the SAVE system, but several Republican-led state governments have voluntarily opted to use the database.

Still, it was not immediately clear if Friday’s decision would have any meaningful impact on the midterm elections on November 3, in which voters will determine which parties control the US House of Representatives and the Senate.

Existing law blocks most states from systematically purging voters from their rolls within 90 days of an election. The emergency order is not also the final say on the matter, only granting the administration the ability to use the system until the court makes a final ruling.

The three liberal justices on the panel, which has a 6-3 conservative supermajority, issued a dissenting opinion, saying the majority disregarded “the harms that the modified SAVE system has caused, and will likely continue to cause, to lawful voters”.

The Citizens for Ethics watchdog group charged that the decision “puts millions of Americans at risk of being unlawfully targeted by the admin’s unreliable voter purge system weeks before the midterms”.

Trump has focused heavily on election administration in the run-up to the midterm vote, which could serve as a major check on his authority in the final two years of his term.

He has for years claimed, without evidence, that US elections are marred by widespread fraud and has repeatedly falsely claimed the 2020 presidential election, which he lost to Democrat Joe Biden, was “stolen”.

Evidence has suggested that fraud of any kind, including instances of non-citizens voting in the US, has been glancingly rare in the country.

In September, the Supreme Court rejected a bid from Trump to restrict mail ballot procedures before the midterm election.

articles.title: Two arrests made after men emerged from New York City sewers
articles.summary: The city has seen a string of incidents in which people have climbed out of manholes late at night.
articles.body:
New York officials arrested two of three men who they said were seen emerging from a manhole, exiting the city's underground sewer system on Wednesday.

The New York Police Department (NYPD) arrested 26-year-old Kevin Rodriguez and 25-year-old Samuel Reveron on charges of conspiracy and trespassing.

Three men were seen exiting a manhole near the hotel where Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu was reportedly expected to stay for the United Nations General Assembly.

In a statement to the BBC, the NYPD said it had seen a number of incidents involving people going into the sewer system to look for valuables and scrap metal after a storm.

"This incident fits that same criteria, but out of an abundance of caution given the U.N. General Assembly and the sensitivity of the location, the NYPD is conducting additional security sweeps with our federal partners," the police department said in a statement.

Rodriguez and Reveron, both from Queens, were arrested on Thursday. They allegedly fled the scene after climbing out of the manhole when officers were called around 4:30 EST (9:30 BST) on Wednesday, police said.

During a hearing on Friday morning, the two men pleaded not guilty and were released from custody, according to court records.

The arrests follow a string of incidents in which people were seen emerging from pavement manholes in different parts of the city in recent months.

In August, surveillance footage showed a person coming out of a manhole in Queens early in the morning. The same month, the NYPD said it was investigating three people wearing overalls and headlamps seen climbing out of a manhole near Penn Station.

In May, a group of people were captured on surveillance footage shifting a manhole cover and climbing down into the sewer in South Brooklyn.

Going into the New York sewer system is both illegal and dangerous, officials have said, cautioning that there is a risk of toxic gases and flooding in a confined space.

"For these reasons, members of the public should never enter a pipe, drain, catch basin, manhole, or outfall," the city's Department of Environmental Protection previously told the BBC.

This year, a woman died after she opened her car door and accidentally fell into an open manhole in Midtown Manhattan.

articles.title: Poland boosts air defence after ‘Russian provocations’ amid Ukraine war
articles.summary: Alleged incursions put NATO nations on alert as Ukraine launches strikes on Russia during parliamentary voting.
articles.body:
Poland has heightened its air defence posture, following repeated alleged incursions into its airspace in recent weeks.

The Polish Air Force launched preventive air patrols on September 17 aimed at securing the eastern part of Polish airspace.

Warsaw officially blamed Russia, but Moscow has denied allegations that it is targeting NATO nations.

“Following the latest Russian provocations and acts of aggression, I have made the decision to expand the protection of our airspace. We are increasing the activity of our air forces, including F-16 aircraft and helicopters,” wrote Polish Defence Minister Wladyslaw Kosiniak-Kamysz on social media.

Those patrols came with a political warning.

“I want to present to the public the most probable scenario for the next few months, because it is a scenario that assumes serious events and requires focus, seriousness and the mental readiness to pass difficult exams,” said Prime Minister Donald Tusk.

“According to intelligence, the Russian plan also includes hybrid drone and missile strikes against countries supporting Ukraine, including Poland,” he said in parliament. “These possibilities have been mentioned for a long time, and today the information is very consistent and, unfortunately, convincing.”

He said the aim of suspected Russian incursions was “to weaken the motivation of NATO countries to apply NATO regulations in the event of aggression against any member state”.

Days later, on September 23, Poland said an Mi-8 helicopter entered Polish airspace from Kaliningrad for 42 seconds.

“Russia is once again testing the readiness of our air defence,” said Poland’s Armed Forces Operational Command.

The most serious Polish claim of a violation was by a Russian Su-24 reconnaissance aircraft in the Baltic Sea in February 2025, an incident Russia reportedly acknowledged.

During the past week, suspected Russian drones were shot down twice in Moldova, and once in Romania on September 24, observers said.

Poland and Romania are two NATO members immediately bordering Ukraine through which military supplies and Western officials have reached Ukraine. Hungary is also a NATO member bordering Ukraine, but has not allowed military supplies through its territory.

The latest alleged airspace violations have again raised the spectre of an open Russian attack on NATO territory, a prospect European intelligence chiefs have been warning about since January 2024.

Czech intelligence chief Michal Koudelka this week told The Guardian that a Russian attack, which “could involve a limited incursion, false-flag provocations, [or] a massive influence campaign”, might come in a matter of “months, not years”.

During the past week, Russian officials made claims to have captured towns in the eastern Ukrainian Donetsk region.

Russia’s Ministry of Defence said on September 19 Moscow’s forces had seized 5,300 square kilometres (2,050 square miles) and more than 220 settlements in Ukraine since the start of 2026.

Moscow launched drone strikes against Ukrainian cities every night of the week, and combined them with missiles on September 19, 22 and 24, killing at least eight people and injuring dozens. One of those deaths was a cleric at a monastery in Kherson. Two were killed when Russia launched three waves of ballistic missiles at Kyiv, including a maternity clinic.

“Since the beginning of this year, Russia has used more than 2,100 missiles of various types against Ukraine. More than 950 of these were ballistic missiles,” Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy told the United Nations General Assembly. During the same period, Russia launched 63,000 drones into the country, he said.

“We need to slow it down before we move to the next stage,” he said. “Because next year, there is a real possibility that AI – not just humans – will begin to decide what happens on the battlefield.”

According to the Institute for the Study of War, which assesses territorial changes using geolocated open sources, Russian claims of a serious advance are vastly overstated.

It estimates that Russia has captured a net 147.7sq km (57sq miles) in the first eight months of 2026, its worst performance of the war by far. Ukrainian forces had liberated at least 972.56sq km (375sq miles) from Russian occupation during the same period, it has found.

Those counteroffensives have come near Oleksandrivka, straddling the Donetsk-Zaporizhia border, and around the town of Lyman in northern Donetsk.

The Lyman operation, codenamed Vivaldi, saw 50sq km (20sq miles) liberated in a second phase of the operation in recent days, Ukrainian officials said.

“Artillery and drone systems targeted enemy command posts, communication hubs, logistics, crossings, and reserves. Air defence and electronic warfare systems created a protective shield over the area of combat operations. The blinded enemy was unable to decipher the plan of the operation, and our units consolidated on the liberated lines,” said an announcement from the Third Army Corps commanded by Andriy Biletsky.

Meanwhile, Russian President Vladimir Putin’s United Russia Party triumphed in the Duma elections, raising its majority from 315 seats in the 450-seat body to 355.

Russian officials prejudged the result as a positive referendum on Putin’s war in Ukraine.

“I have no doubt that the result will confirm the commitment of all our parties and voters to the course the president has set both domestically and for our foreign policy,” Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov told reporters ahead of the election.

“We will continue to ensure support for our president’s course and bring victory over the enemies of the Fatherland closer,” deputy chairman of Russia’s Security Council Dmitry Medvedev wrote on Russian social media.

Ukraine launched its biggest combined air strike of the war on the final day of Russia’s parliamentary elections.

Moscow mayor Sergei Sobyanin said on September 20 that Russian air defences downed more than 1,600 Ukrainian drones in the previous 24 hours, at least 450 of them heading for Moscow.

Some got through, putting Moscow’s oil refinery out of action for the second time this year. Videos posted online showed several fires, suggesting a number of successful strikes.

During the past week, Ukraine also struck the Kuybyshev refinery in Samara and the Bashneft refinery in Bashkortostan.
